summary.title: Graph Engineering in the Era of LLM Agents: From Individual Intelligence to System Intelligence

details: Single-agent 'Individual Intelligence' (LLM + Harness + Loop) cannot handle tasks requiring heterogeneous expertise, interdependent/parallel subtasks, independent verification, and persistent state, because everything is forced into one context and one sequential control trajectory.
Simply adding more agents does not yield system-level capability without explicit structures for organizing work, coordinating agents, and managing state.

Proposes 'Graph Engineering': an engineering paradigm in which explicit, dynamic, evolving graph structures serve as the operational substrate for organizing tasks, agents, and runtime states, positioned as the successor to Prompt, Context, Harness, and Loop Engineering.

Organized around three coupled graph views: Task Organization (goal decomposition + workflow optimization), Agent Coordination (capability modeling, team organization, communication), and Runtime State Management (state recording, fault localization, failure recovery), plus a cross-execution System Evolution loop.

Introduces 'System Intelligence' as the target capability: decomposing objectives, allocating work across heterogeneous agents, coordinating interdependent execution, and maintaining system-level state.

Traces a progression: parameter-level training (pre-/post-training) → Prompt & Context Engineering (Model Intelligence) → Harness & Loop Engineering (Individual Intelligence) → Graph Engineering (System Intelligence).
Formalizes Agent = Loop(LLM + Harness); Harness supplies tools, memory, skills, runtime orchestration; Loop covers loop architecture, interaction paradigm, environment feedback.
Sections cover preliminaries, evolution of intelligence levels, the three-view Graph Engineering taxonomy, challenges/future directions, benchmarks, open-source libraries, and applications.
Task Organization: HuggingGPT, ReWOO, LLMCompiler, Plan-over-Graph, TDAG, Flow, GPTSwarm, ADAS, AFlow/A2Flow, MermaidFlow, VFlow, DyFlow, EvoFlow, QualityFlow, FlowSteer.

Agent Coordination: DyLAN, MasRouter, AutoAgents, EvoAgent, Captain Agent, SkillGraph, MaAS, MetaGPT, ChatDev, Magentic-One, Mixture-of-Agents, MacNet, AgentNet, SwarmAgentic, G-Designer, AgentPrune, AgentDropout, DyTopo, CARD.

Runtime State Management: Magentic-One ledgers, Graph of States, PatchBoard, MemTX, Collaborative Memory, event sourcing/'The Log is the Agent', MAGE, Who&When, MAST, TraceElephant, TDAD, Cordon, AgentGit, Shepherd, DART, SagaLLM, Atomix, Aegis.

Three concrete limitations enumerated: serialization of parallelizable/interdependent subtasks (e.g. software fault diagnosis branches), lack of stable specialized roles and independent verification (self-evaluation confirmation bias), and unstructured non-persistent state making early errors undetectable and unrecoverable in long-horizon tasks.
Ontology Engineering proposed as the semantic layer to give consistent, machine-interpretable definitions of entities/relations across graph views, enabling reuse and validation.

Argues end-task success is insufficient evidence of System Intelligence; proposes evaluating semantic consistency, parallel efficiency, capability allocation, state consistency, recovery, transfer, and runtime overhead via intervention studies, structural ablations, and execution-trace analysis under stress conditions (component failures, concurrency, distributed information).

key_findings.finding: The paper articulates Graph Engineering as a distinct engineering paradigm succeeding Prompt, Context, Harness, and Loop Engineering, with graphs as operational rather than merely representational structures.
key_findings.evidence: A taxonomy positions each paradigm along a progression from Model Intelligence to Individual Intelligence to System Intelligence, and defines Graph Engineering by three organizational problems (task organization, agent coordination, runtime state management) that single-agent paradigms structurally cannot address.

key_findings.finding: Individual Intelligence fails on complex tasks for architectural rather than capability reasons, so scaling context or model strength cannot fix it.
key_findings.evidence: Three structural bottlenecks are identified and illustrated: forced serialization of parallel/interdependent branches, absence of stable role separation leading to self-verification bias, and non-persistent unstructured context that prevents fault localization and partial recovery in long-horizon runs.

key_findings.finding: Runtime state management is identified as the least-developed pillar, with existing systems covering fragments of state recording, fault localization, and recovery but no unified graph-native implementation.
key_findings.evidence: The survey decomposes reliable state into structured representation, governed updates (proposal-validation-commit as in PatchBoard/MemTX), scoped visibility, and concurrency consistency, and shows recovery work splits between replay/rollback (event sourcing, AgentGit, DART) and compensation for irreversible external effects (SagaLLM, Atomix), concluding no system integrates these.

key_findings.finding: System Evolution—using execution evidence to revise task graphs, team/communication topologies, and accumulated state—is emerging but remains fragile and rare in deployed applications.
key_findings.evidence: Evolution is documented across the three views (TDAG/DyFlow/EvoFlow for tasks, SwarmAgentic/AgentNet/DyTopo/CARD for coordination, ReCreate/SkillGraph/MemTX for state), while FlowSteer shows manipulated planning signals can steer replanning toward harmful paths, and the application review reports persistent System Evolution is still limited in practice.

key_findings.finding: Ontology Engineering is proposed as the necessary semantic complement to Graph Engineering for next-generation systems.
key_findings.evidence: The paper argues that existing graph approaches assume shared meanings for goals, operations, capabilities, and states—an assumption that breaks in open, long-running, industrial settings—and surveys ontology work (AgentO, OntoCodex, Palantir Ontology, etc.) as the basis for connecting, validating, and evolving graph structures.
